newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia revels in glory of solo sailor rescues.
newsitem.headline: Australia revels in glory of solo sailor rescues.

text.p: A search was under way on Friday for a missing Canadian yachtsman in a remote Antarctica area as Australia revelled in the dramatic rescue of two other round-the-world sailors.
The rescue of the pair -- a Briton and a Frenchman -- brought warm praise from Britain and the chance that relations with France could be buoyed by the success.
"This is a great story in the annals of sailing," acting prime minister Tim Fischer said on Australian radio.
"I think it has been an Australian privilege to fulfill the role it has been obliged to fulfill," he said.

However, as an Australian navy frigate headed back to port with Briton Tony Bullimore and Frenchman Thierry Dubois safely aboard, race organisers were coordinating a search for a Canadian yachtsman feared to be in trouble.
Other competitors in the Vendee Globe round-the-world sailing race were closing in on a remote stretch of the Antarctic where Canadian Gerry Roufs was last heard from several days ago.
The successful four-day hunt for solo sailors Bullimore and Dubois raised Australia's profile in Europe and brought tributes for rescue services, with messages of thanks from France and Britain.
It has been seen by some as a chance to improve Australia's sometimes squally relationship with France after last year's row over nuclear testing in the Pacific.

French President Jacques Chirac warmly praised Australia's efforts, singling out Australian Ambassador John Spender at his New Year reception at the Elysee Palace, the Australian Financial Review reported on Friday.
"He greeted Mr Spender warmly and spoke to him at length, to the surprise and delight of Australian officials," the newspaper reported.

The rescues increased the prospect of a visit to Australia this year by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who would be the first French foreign minister to visit the country, the newspaper said.

British Prime Minister John Major, now on a trip to India, offered his thanks to the Australian rescuers while Queen Elizabeth -- who many Australians want to dump as the country's titular head of state -- also sent congratulations.
French sailor Dubois was plucked from a life raft by helicopter at first light on Thursday.
Hours later, Bullimore, whose fate was unknown for five days, swam into the arms of rescuers from beneath his upturned yacht.

The two men, who capsized in wild storms on Sunday, were competing in the Vendee Globe race, which had already seen the rescue the day after Christmas of French sailor Raphael Dinelli from his sinking yacht.

Australia's rescue two years ago of Frenchwoman Isabelle Autissier, which cost about A$745,000 above the normal operating costs of the ships and aircraft involved, led to a public outcry over the cost.
However, politicians this time are stressing the country's international and moral obligations in the latest operations.

"We have done what is required and we would do it again, whenever necessary," said Defence Minister Ian McLachlan after Dubois was winched to safety. McLachlan said such rescues provided experience for defence forces.
Australia has, however, raised the question of safety.
Sports minister Warwick Smith said he had written to his French counterpart Guy Drut asking him to help put pressure on sailing authorities to make racing safer.
"Specifically, I would suggest competitors take a longer, more northerly and therefore safer route," he wrote to Drut.
An Australian meteorologist on Friday also suggested round-the-world races should engage a mother ship which could come to the aid of competitors.
"Strong winds and nasty storms and seas can develop at all latitudes in the Southern Ocean," Roger Badham, a consultant on ocean racing events, said on Australian radio.
Others have criticised yacht design, but retired solo sailor Ian Johnston, a friend of Bullimore's for 15 years, said there was no way to stop such races.
"You can't stop people climbing Mount Everest," he said. "This is the Everest of sailing."
